Executive Overview and Macro-Fiscal Architecture of the SR&ED Regime

Canada operates one of the most comprehensive and fiscally significant research and development tax incentive frameworks in the industrialized world through the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Jointly architected at the policy level by the Department of Finance Canada and administered operationally by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the SR&ED regime functions as the cornerstone of the federal government's industrial innovation strategy. During the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle, the CRA approved $4.6 billion in federal investment tax credits across 23,677 processed claims, marking a substantial expansion from historical baselines of approximately 16,000 to 19,000 corporate filings and $2.7 billion to $3.0 billion in annual tax relief. Across the national claimant base in 2025–2026, 59% of all allowed investment tax credits were disbursed as refundable credits—providing direct non-dilutive liquidity to innovating enterprises regardless of current tax liability—while 41% were claimed as non-refundable credits applied against Part I federal tax payable. Sectoral data from the CRA demonstrates a structural shift toward digital and computational research, with software development accounting for 42.6% of all allowed investment tax credits in 2025–2026, up from 35.7% in 2021–2022. This trajectory reflects the increasing dominance of artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure engineering, and complex algorithmic systems within the Canadian innovation economy, prompting heightened scrutiny from CRA technical auditors regarding the boundary between routine software development and genuine experimental development.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade with the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Applying retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 fundamentally recalibrated the economic parameters of the federal SR&ED regime. While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement had initially proposed an intermediate increase of the enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million (yielding a $1.575 million refundable ceiling), the final enacted provisions of Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million, elevating the maximum annual federal cash refund ceiling from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Concurrently, Bill C-15 expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10 million to $50 million corridor to an expanded $15 million to $75 million corridor, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) utilizing a gross revenue phase-out test, allowed Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to elect into that same gross revenue phase-out structure, and restored the eligibility of depreciable capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024.

At the sub-national level, the federal SR&ED baseline integrates with an intricate matrix of provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants. Because provincial incentives generally piggyback on the federal definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act while simultaneously constituting "government assistance" that reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d), the effective combined recovery rate requires iterative multi-jurisdictional modelling. Notably, Quebec executed a structural overhaul of its provincial innovation regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating four legacy R&D tax credit programmes into the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which offers a universal two-tier 30% and 20% refundable rate structure alongside a reformed employee-prorated exclusion threshold and modernized E-Business (CDAE and CDAEIA) parameters.

body.text: Statutory Foundation and Legislative Evolution Under the Income Tax Act

The legal architecture of the Canadian federal R&D tax incentive system is codified within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), current to October 19, 2026 and last amended on June 18, 2026, alongside Part XXIX (Section 2900) and Part XLVI (Section 4606) of the Income Tax Regulations. The statutory regime operates through a dual-benefit mechanism that separates tax deductibility from tax credit monetization. First, Section 37 provides an immediate or indefinitely carry-forwardable income deduction for allowable SR&ED expenditures pooled at the taxpayer level, reducing net income for tax purposes. Second, Section 127 calculates an Investment Tax Credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures that offsets Part I federal income tax payable, while Section 127.1 governs the monetization of unused credits as a direct cash refund for qualifying taxpayers.
Subsection 248(1) Definition of SR&ED and Statutory Exclusions

The gateway to both federal and provincial R&D tax relief is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which generally conforms to the international OECD Frascati Manual baseline while maintaining specific Canadian statutory contours. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". This overarching preamble is operationalized by the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives into two mandatory requirements that must both be met for work to qualify: the "Why" requirement, which demands that the work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement to overcome scientific or technological uncertainty; and the "How" requirement, which requires a systematic investigation or search involving the formulation of an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts, testing that hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, developing logical conclusions based on the resulting findings, and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

Within the architecture of subsection 248(1), eligible core and supporting activities are categorized into four statutory paragraphs. Paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(b) covers applied research, which comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(c) codifies experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Across Canadian corporate filings, the overwhelming majority of industrial, manufacturing, and software claims are adjudicated under paragraph 248(1)(c), though the CRA recognizes that given the similarity between experimental development and applied research—both having a practical application in view—many characteristics of experimental development extend directly to applied research. Finally, paragraph 248(1)(d) authorizes eligible support work, which consists of work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustively enumerated disciplines—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

A nuanced understanding of CRA policy evolution is essential when evaluating engineering and knowledge-acquisition activities under subsection 248(1). Effective April 24, 2015, the CRA removed the term "routine engineering" from its official glossary definitions on the grounds that there is no lexical differentiation between engineering and routine engineering in the statute; instead, the CRA clarified that while engineering practice on its own is not eligible, engineers routinely perform eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development, or perform paragraph (d) engineering support work commensurate with and directly supporting such experimental development. Furthermore, CRA guidelines explicitly establish that acquiring available knowledge or know-how—such as through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or external consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge and licences—does not meet the statutory requirement of attempting to achieve a scientific or technological advancement. Rather, a claimant must confront a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty arising from a limitation in the "scientific or technological knowledge base," which consists of the combined knowledge of the resources within the business and all sources that are reasonably available publicly.

To establish firm statutory boundaries against commercial or non-scientific activities, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the Income Tax Act codify seven explicit exclusions—collectively termed "excluded work" or "the exclusions"—that cannot be claimed as SR&ED under any circumstances. Specifically, paragraph 248(1)(e) excludes market research or sales promotion; paragraph 248(1)(f) excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; paragraph 248(1)(g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities; paragraph 248(1)(h) excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; paragraph 248(1)(i) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; paragraph 248(1)(j) excludes style changes; and paragraph 248(1)(k) excludes routine data collection. In audit adjudication, the CRA instructs Research and Technology Advisors that excluded work should only be considered after identifying that eligible SR&ED work has been performed, serving to carve out ineligible concurrent activities—for example, where a mining company conducts eligible metallurgical process SR&ED while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the prospecting work must be severed and excluded under paragraph (h). When an activity such as data collection or testing appears in both paragraph (d) as eligible support work and paragraphs (f) or (k) as excluded work, the determinative legal criterion is purpose: if data collection or testing is carried out specifically to perform and directly support the experimental development, it qualifies under paragraph 248(1)(d); if it is performed for commercial production validation, standard quality assurance, or another commercial reason, it is barred by paragraphs (f), (i), or (k).
Section 37 Expenditure Pool Mechanics and Section 127 Investment Tax Credit Architecture

Once technical activities satisfy the requirements of subsection 248(1), the financial accounting and tax monetization of the associated costs flow sequentially through Section 37 and Section 127 of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 37(1) establishes a cumulative tax pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures incurred by a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Subsection 37(8) sets out the interpretive rules governing which specific expenditures in respect of SR&ED are eligible for inclusion in the subsection 37(1) pool, while subsection 37(1.1) provides that, where the taxpayer is a corporation, SR&ED related to a business of a related corporation may be treated as related to a business of the taxpayer. Additionally, subsection 37(11) imposes the prescribed-form filing requirement, which operates alongside subsection 37(1) and paragraph 127(9)(m).

The subsection 37(1) deductible pool aggregates allowable current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a)—comprising direct in-house SR&ED expenditures, eligible contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), and third-party payments to corporations or approved research entities under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)—alongside restored capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) and repayments of prior government or non-government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(c). This cumulative pool is mandatorily reduced under paragraphs 37(1)(d) and 37(1)(d.1) by any government assistance, non-government assistance, contract payments, and provincial super-allowance benefit amounts that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. Furthermore, federal investment tax credits claimed against tax payable or received as a cash refund in a given taxation year reduce the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year, or are included directly in taxable income in the following year under paragraph 12(1)(t) if the pool is driven negative, thereby preventing a double tax benefit on the same dollar of expenditure. Claimants are not compelled to deduct their entire Section 37 pool balance (calculated on Line 455 of Form T661) in the taxation year incurred; the deduction is entirely optional, and any undeducted pool balance carries forward indefinitely to offset business income on T2 Schedule 1 in future taxation years, although a corporation that undergoes an acquisition of control may face statutory loss-streaming restrictions limiting its ability to deduct the Line 455 pool balance in the year of acquisition or subsequent taxation years.

Operating in parallel with the Section 37 income deduction pool, Section 127 governs the computation of the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" and the resulting Investment Tax Credit. Unlike the Section 37 deductible pool, which carries forward indefinitely from year to year, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool defined under subsection 127(9) is calculated strictly on an annual basis at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over to another taxation year. Qualified expenditures calculated on Line 559 and Line 570 of Form T661 are transferred to Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) or Form T2038-IND (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)), where the statutory credit rates of 35% or 15% are applied to generate the annual ITC.
Bill C-15 Legislative Reforms and Effective Transition Rules (2024–2026)

The passage of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, formally titled An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted the largest structural expansion of the SR&ED programme in over ten years. Designed by the Department of Finance Canada to reverse a decade-long decline in Canadian business enterprise R&D intensity and prevent capital-intensive scale-up companies from relocating innovation activities abroad after going public, Bill C-15 introduced four major legislative pillars whose effective transition dates must be carefully distinguished during tax compliance and audit reviews.

First, Bill C-15 doubled the baseline annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit from $3 million to $6 million, increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit from $1.05 million to $2.1 million for taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Second, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the legislation widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor for CCPCs from the legacy $10 million to $50 million range to a substantially broader $15 million to $75 million range, while simultaneously granting CCPCs an elective option to have their expenditure limit phase-out determined using an average gross revenue test ($15 million to $75 million) rather than taxable capital. Third, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), eliminating the punitive tax cliff that historically stripped Canadian technology and energy firms of refundable SR&ED support the moment they listed on a public stock exchange.

Fourth, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of depreciable capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), reversing the repeal that had been in effect since January 1, 2014. Crucially, unlike the $6 million expenditure limit, phase-out threshold, and ECPC amendments—which apply only to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—the restoration of capital expenditures applies on a transaction-date basis to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that becomes available for use after that date. Consequently, if a corporation's taxation year straddles December 15, 2024 (having begun on or before December 15, 2024), the corporation remains bound by the $3 million expenditure limit and pre-Bill C-15 entity rules for that straddle year, but it is immediately entitled to claim SR&ED capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, calculating the property's SR&ED operating-time percentage strictly over the post-December 15, 2024 portion of the taxation year. Conversely, expenditures for depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024 generally do not qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, although specialized tax practitioners closely examine the interaction with amended subsection 127(11.2) of the Income Tax Act—the time-of-acquisition deeming rule for subsections 127(5), 127(7), and 127(8)—which deems property not to have been acquired until it becomes "available for use," potentially allowing ITC claims on long-lead capital equipment ordered prior to December 16, 2024 that first became available for use after December 15, 2024.
Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Carry-Over Rules

The financial value of a federal SR&ED claim is governed by a strict statutory classification of the taxpayer under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. Rather than operating on a progressive or sliding rate schedule, the federal regime applies one of two flat credit rates—the enhanced 35% rate or the basic 15% rate (which was reduced from 20% after 2013)—while varying the expenditure limit and the refundability percentage according to corporate status, ownership control, capital or revenue size, and current versus capital expenditure classification.
Claimant Classifications: CCPCs, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, and Other Entities

Every taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs SR&ED in Canada is eligible to participate in the federal regime, including resident companies and domestic Canadian branches of non-resident corporations, provided the expenditures are incurred for domestic R&D carried on in Canada rather than at foreign branches. However, the applicable ITC rate and cash refundability rules segregate claimants into four primary legal categories.

Qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)—defined as private corporations resident in Canada that are not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons, one or more public corporations, or any combination thereof—represent the primary beneficiaries of the enhanced regime. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a qualifying CCPC earns the enhanced 35% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit of $6 million (up from $3 million in prior taxation years). Under Section 127.1, the 35% ITC earned within the $6 million expenditure limit is 100% refundable on current expenditures—generating up to $2.1 million in direct cash refunds even for pre-revenue startups with zero tax liability—and 40% refundable on eligible post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures. Qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC above its $6 million expenditure limit earn the basic 15% ITC; while this excess credit is generally non-refundable for larger CCPCs, a qualifying CCPC that satisfies its size thresholds can earn 40% refundability on the 15% basic credit attributable to current expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) constitute the second claimant tier, established by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC at any time in the taxation year, a corporation must be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected or been designated to be a public corporation), and not be controlled by non-resident persons. An ECPC earns the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on the first $6 million of qualified current SR&ED expenditures—allowing domestic public companies to claim up to $2.1 million annually in refundable cash credits—subject to a phase-out based solely on prior-period gross revenue. Any qualified expenditures incurred by an ECPC in excess of its expenditure limit earn the non-refundable 15% basic ITC.

Other corporations—comprising foreign-controlled private subsidiaries (such as Canadian R&D subsidiaries owned by United States, European, or Asian parent corporations), Canadian public corporations controlled by non-residents, and domestic public or private corporations whose revenue or taxable capital exceeds the $75 million phase-out ceiling—do not have an expenditure limit and earn the basic 15% ITC on 100% of their qualified SR&ED expenditures. For this corporate category, the 15% ITC is strictly non-refundable and can only be utilized to offset federal Part I income tax payable in the current year or via carryback and carryforward provisions.

Finally, unincorporated individuals (sole proprietorships), beneficiaries of trusts, and members of partnerships are governed by specialized flow-through and partial refundability rules. Individuals and trusts earn the basic 15% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures with no enhanced rate tier; however, under Section 127.1, 40% of any unused 15% credit remaining after offsetting current-year Part I tax payable is refundable in cash. Partnerships are not taxable entities and cannot claim an ITC in their own right. Instead, a partnership files Form T661 to compute the partnership's SR&ED expenditures, deducts the Section 37 expenditure pool in computing partnership net income, and allocates the resulting qualified expenditures or ITCs under subsection 127(8) to its active partners (excluding specified members or passive limited partners), who then claim the credit on their respective corporate (Schedule T2SCH31) or individual (Form T2038-IND) returns at the rate and refundability percentage corresponding to each partner's legal status. Where all members of a partnership throughout a taxation year are CCPCs, or where a CCPC or shareholder of a CCPC is a member, Section 127.1 preserves CCPC refundable ITC mechanics on the allocated partnership share.

body.text: Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital and Gross Revenue Mechanics

The $6 million enhanced expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act is an associated-group ceiling, meaning that a corporate group cannot multiply its access to the $2.1 million refundable ITC ceiling by spinning up multiple operating subsidiaries. Associated Canadian-controlled private corporations must file T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) to allocate the group's single expenditure limit among its constituent members.

Prior to the enactment of Bill C-15, a CCPC's $3 million expenditure limit was phased out when the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada for the preceding taxation year rose between $10 million and $50 million (and historically included a prior-year taxable income phase-out between $500,000 and $800,000 that remains active in provincial regimes such as Ontario's OITC). Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline federal expenditure limit of $6 million is reduced on a linear basis when the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada for the preceding taxation year exceeds $15 million, reaching zero when taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75 million. Mathematically, for a standard 365-day taxation year (prorated for short taxation years), the post-Bill C-15 CCPC expenditure limit under the default taxable capital test is expressed as:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000

Under this statutory ratio, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15 million reduces the $6 million expenditure limit by $1. By contrast, under the pre-Bill C-15 regime applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the phase-out operated across a $40 million denominator between $10 million and $50 million against a $3 million base, where every $13.33 of taxable capital above $10 million reduced the limit by $1:

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $10,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000

For an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—and for any CCPC that formally elects to use the revenue-based phase-out structure instead of taxable capital—the $6 million baseline expenditure limit is reduced on a linear basis according to the corporation's (and its associated or consolidated corporate group's) average gross revenue over the preceding three taxation years between $15 million and $75 million:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if average annual gross revenue for the three preceding fiscal years is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average exceeds $15,000,000

This elective gross revenue pathway represents a vital tax planning mechanism for capital-intensive private corporations—such as clinical-stage biotechnology firms, clean-technology developers, aerospace startups, and advanced hardware manufacturers—that accumulate large balance-sheet equity or debt balances exceeding $15 million or $75 million in taxable capital to finance multi-year R&D programmes while generating minimal or zero commercial revenue. By electing into the gross revenue phase-out structure, a high-capital, pre-revenue CCPC completely avoids the taxable capital grind and preserves its full $6 million expenditure limit and $2.1 million annual refundable cash credit.
Refundability Tiers, Carryback/Carryforward Horizons, and Recapture Taxation

When an Investment Tax Credit is computed on Schedule T2SCH31, the Income Tax Act enforces a mandatory sequence of utilization. First, under subsection 127(5), the generated ITC must be applied to reduce the taxpayer's federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Second, if unused ITC balances remain after extinguishing current Part I tax payable, qualifying claimants may elect to monetize the excess as a cash refund under Section 127.1 up to their statutory refundability ceiling—namely, 100% refundability on current expenditures within the $6 million limit for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs, 40% refundability on capital expenditures within the limit for qualifying CCPCs, and 40% refundability on the 15% basic credit for qualifying CCPCs above the limit as well as unincorporated individuals and trusts. Third, any non-refundable ITC balance—or any refundable ITC that a taxpayer chooses not to have refunded—may be carried back 3 taxation years to recover federal Part I income tax paid in prior profitable years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset future federal Part I tax liabilities.

A fundamental second-order fiscal effect of the Canadian regime is the statutory taxation of SR&ED tax relief. Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Income Tax Act, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed to offset Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund in a given taxation year reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the following taxation year; if that reduction exceeds the available Section 37 pool balance in the following year, the negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(t) in that subsequent year. Consequently, while a pre-revenue CCPC in a tax-loss position experiences no immediate cash tax leakage from the paragraph 12(1)(t) inclusion, a profitable CCPC paying corporate tax must account for the deferred tax cost on the ITC in the following fiscal year. In contrast to the federal ITC (which reduces the pool with a one-year lag), provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants (such as the Ontario OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC, the Quebec CRIC, the BC SR&ED credit, and the Alberta IEG) constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) in the current taxation year, reducing both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base in the same year the provincial credit is earned.

Furthermore, with the reintroduction of capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment after December 15, 2024 under Bill C-15, the statutory SR&ED ITC Recapture regime under subsections 127(27) through 127(35) has returned to active enforcement. If a taxpayer claims an SR&ED ITC on a depreciable capital property (or transfers qualified expenditures under a non-arm's-length agreement) and subsequently sells the property or converts it to commercial (non-SR&ED) use within the statutory recapture window, the taxpayer must calculate the ITC recapture amount—generally the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property and the applicable credit percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition or fair market value at conversion—using Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or Form T2038-IND for individuals (including members of partnerships) and add the recaptured amount directly to Part I Tax Payable for the taxation year of disposition or conversion, alongside any applicable Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) recapture.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Cost Base Substantiation Rules

Under subsection 127(9) and Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, only specific, statutorily defined expenditure categories incurred in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada qualify for inclusion in the SR&ED cost base. Any R&D activity performed outside Canada is ineligible for the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit, subject only to a narrow statutory exception under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permitting permissible salary or wages of Canadian-resident employees travelling outside Canada to perform direct SR&ED activities, capped at 10% of the claimant's total directly engaged Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages.
Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Restrictions (YMPE Caps)

Salaries and wages constitute the single largest expenditure component across Canadian SR&ED claims. To qualify, salary or wages must be incurred for employees of the claimant who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED refers strictly to hands-on technical execution and direct first-line technical supervision of experiments or analysis; eligibility is determined solely by the actual technical tasks performed by the individual rather than job titles or corporate rank. All claimed remuneration must represent employment income reported on a T4 slip—comprising regular salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave, and taxable benefits (plus employer portions of CPP/QPP, EI, QPIP, and provincial payroll health or workers' compensation levies when claiming under the traditional overhead method, whereas retiring allowances are excluded)—while dividends, shareholder draws, or management fees paid outside T4 payroll are strictly ineligible. Additionally, under subsection 127(26) and subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary, wages, or other remuneration incurred in a taxation year that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is excluded from qualified expenditures for that year (reported on Line 315 of Form T661) and can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid.

A critical audit trap involves the statutory restrictions governing "specified employees". Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a specified employee is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the corporation—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or any corporation related to it—or an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder). To prevent closely held corporations from inflating refundable SR&ED credits by paying massive year-end bonuses or above-market salaries to founder-shareholders, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations enforce two distinct statutory ceilings on specified employee remuneration.

First, under subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1) of the Income Tax Act, when computing direct SR&ED salary expenditures in Part 3 of Form T661, all remuneration based on profits or bonuses paid to a specified employee is 100% disallowed, and the remaining salary or wages that may be claimed for the specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) established under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year in which the person was a specified employee. Second, under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations, when computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661, the includable salary of each specified employee is restricted even further to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary and wages for the year (less bonuses and taxable benefits), or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year, prorated for short taxation years. Furthermore, where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in the same year, both the 5x YMPE direct salary ceiling and the 2.5x YMPE proxy salary base ceiling must be shared and allocated among the associated corporations by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).
Overhead Costing Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Versus Traditional Method

Claimants must elect on Part 1 of Form T661 between two mutually exclusive methodologies for capturing SR&ED overhead costs for the entire taxation year; once the election is submitted with the initial Form T661 for that taxation year, it is irrevocable for that year.

The Prescribed Proxy Method, codified under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and detailed in the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, is elected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants, particularly in the software, information technology, and engineering sectors. Under the proxy method, the claimant does not include specific overhead expenses inside the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool (instead deducting ordinary overhead expenses under general business income rules in Section 18 of the Income Tax Act), and calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Part 5 and Line 502 of Form T661 strictly for the purpose of earning Section 127 Investment Tax Credits. The PPA equals a flat 55% of the claimant's eligible SR&ED "salary base"—comprising the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, and unpaid amounts, and capped by the 2.5x YMPE / 75% specified employee limit under Regulation 2900(7)). For example, $430,000 in qualifying non-specified developer salaries automatically generates $236,500 in proxy overhead ($430,000 × 55%) without requiring item-by-item overhead tracking. Crucially, the 55% PPA is computed exclusively on T4 employee salaries and never applies to subcontractor fees. When electing the proxy method, claimants are statutorily barred from claiming lease costs or capital expenditures for general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), and the notional PPA is subject to an overall ceiling ensuring that the sum of the PPA and other qualified expenditures does not exceed total business operating deductions.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the 55% notional proxy and instead tracks, substantiates, and claims actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under the traditional method, eligible Line 360 costs include non-directly-engaged support staff tasks that directly support SR&ED, incremental utilities (such as high-voltage electricity or industrial gases for test rigs), maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED facilities or equipment, and—under the Bill C-15 rules effective for expenses incurred after December 15, 2024—lease costs for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time (claimed on Line 360) alongside lease costs for equipment used 90% or more (ASA) in SR&ED (claimed on Lines 350 and 355 and detailed by project in Part 6A, Box 759). Because the traditional method requires rigorous cost-accounting apportionment and contemporaneous proof of direct nexus for every overhead dollar, it is generally utilized only by capital-intensive industrial, chemical, or manufacturing taxpayers whose facility and utility overhead exceeds 55% of their direct SR&ED payroll.
Arm's-Length Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transactions, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages external parties to conduct R&D in Canada, the Income Tax Act applies distinct statutory rules depending on whether the transaction is an arm's-length SR&ED contract, a non-arm's-length contract or purchase, or a third-party payment.

For arm's-length Canadian SR&ED contracts (reported on Line 340 of Form T661), payments made to a Canadian contractor dealing at arm's length with the claimant for basic research, applied research, experimental development, or paragraph 248(1)(d) support work performed on behalf of the claimant in Canada are 100% deductible in the Section 37 expenditure pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), but only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in qualified expenditures for Section 127 Investment Tax Credit purposes (reflecting a statutory 20% haircut enacted after 2012 to remove the contractor's assumed profit margin). Thus, an eligible arm's-length Canadian contractor invoice of $142,500 contributes $114,000 ($142,500 × 80%) to the claimant's qualified expenditure base. To withstand CRA audit scrutiny, the claimant must retain statements of work and itemized invoices demonstrating that the contractor physically performed the SR&ED inside Canada—as payments to United States or offshore foreign development shops are 100% ineligible for SR&ED credits—and that the work was performed on the claimant's behalf with the claimant retaining ownership or exploitation rights.

Non-arm's-length (NAL) contracts and purchases (evaluated under Section 251 of the Income Tax Act and reported on Line 345, Line 510, Line 540, Line 543, and Line 546 of Form T661) are governed by anti-avoidance provisions in subsections 127(11.5), 127(11.6), and 127(13) through 127(15). When a claimant pays a non-arm's-length party (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation) to perform an SR&ED contract, the payment does not qualify directly for ITCs in the hands of the payer. Instead, the NAL performer claims the underlying SR&ED expenditures it incurred, and the two related parties may execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (reported on Line 540 / Line 546 of the performer's Form T661 and Line 510 of the payer's Form T661) up to the contract price, thereby eliminating any intercompany markup from the ITC calculation. Similarly, where a claimant purchases goods, services, or post-December 15, 2024 capital property from a non-arm's-length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) deems the expenditure not to exceed the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier, and the difference between the intercompany invoice price and the deemed cost must be subtracted on Line 543 of Form T661.

Third-party payments (codified under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) and reported on Line 370 of Form T661 alongside Form T1263, Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) represent payments made by a claimant to an approved association, university, college, research institute, or non-profit R&D organization for SR&ED carried on in Canada where the claimant does not direct the day-to-day research (distinguishing it from a direct SR&ED contract), provided the SR&ED is related to a business class of the claimant and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Like arm's-length contracts, 80% of an eligible third-party payment qualifies for the Section 127 ITC, and the amount received by the university or research institute is not treated as a "contract payment" that reduces the institution's own research pool.
Materials Consumed or Transformed and Cloud Computing Infrastructure Segmentation

Direct expenditures for materials (reported on Lines 320 and 325 of Form T661) are 100% includable in both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base if the materials are either "consumed" or "transformed" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under section 5.0 of the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials consumed means the substance or item was destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of the SR&ED experimentation. Materials transformed refers to tangible components integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom build during the experimental process. If a prototype containing transformed materials or any excess production beyond what was required for SR&ED is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC base are subject to cost-recovery recapture rules based on the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value) and the original material expenditure claimed.

In the software, SaaS, and artificial intelligence sectors, the eligibility and accounting treatment of cloud computing expenses (such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform) is a primary focus of contemporary CRA financial reviews. Cloud computing resources utilized directly and exclusively for SR&ED experimentation—such as ephemeral GPU/TPU compute clusters used to train and test experimental deep-learning architectures, or isolated development and staging environments used to benchmark novel distributed systems under scale constraints—are accepted as eligible costs (typically claimed on Line 320 as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED or as directly attributable overhead under the traditional method). However, cloud infrastructure hosting live customer-facing production workloads, commercial SaaS delivery (which belongs in Cost of Goods Sold / Cost of Revenue), or unsegmented corporate hosting is 100% ineligible. To survive a CRA audit, software claimants must implement monthly cloud billing exports with granular resource tags that strictly segregate "production" environments (coded to COGS) from "experimental R&D" environments (coded to specific SR&ED project accounts), as unsegmented lump-sum cloud invoices are routinely disallowed. Additionally, standard commercial software or CAD subscriptions under the proxy method, routine third-party data-provider API fees, and prompt engineering against commercial foundation models do not qualify as SR&ED expenditures.
Restored Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024 Regime)

Following a ten-year hiatus during which capital equipment was completely excluded from SR&ED incentives (January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 restored both full SR&ED capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. Pursuant to the CRA's updated Form T661 (26) instructions and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (issued in May 2026 and updated in October 2026), claimants must distinguish between two statutory capital regimes based on the intensity of SR&ED usage.

The first regime governs All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Property, reported on Line 390 of Form T661. An expenditure for new or used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 qualifies on Line 390 if the property becomes "available for use" after December 15, 2024 and the claimant intended at the time of acquisition that the property would either: (1) be used all or substantially all (defined as 90% or more) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada; or (2) have all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value consumed in performing SR&ED in Canada (such as custom experimental tooling, moulds, CNC prototyping machinery, or dedicated R&D servers bought outright). While both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test are entered on Line 390 and qualify for 100% immediate deduction inside the Section 37 expenditure pool, used equipment does not qualify for the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit and must be subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661. Only new depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA threshold earns the SR&ED ITC, which is 40% refundable for qualifying CCPCs within the $6 million expenditure limit. Furthermore, because Line 390 capital expenditures are deducted through the Section 37 SR&ED pool, they must not be included in Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) classes on Schedule T2SCH8. Non-depreciable property (such as land), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures under all circumstances, and claimants electing the Prescribed Proxy Method cannot include general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) as capital expenditures. Note also that while purchasing an ASA prototyping machine outright after December 15, 2024 qualifies as a capital expenditure (and leasing ASA equipment qualifies under the traditional method), hourly rental or leasing under the proxy method does not enter the capital pool and remains an ordinary business deduction under paragraph 18(1)(a).

The second regime governs Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), reported on Line 504 and Part 6C of Form T661. SUE applies to new depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, and GPOEF under the proxy method) acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA threshold but is used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. Unlike Line 390 ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; instead, the equipment is capitalized and depreciated under ordinary Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8. For Investment Tax Credit purposes, SUE earns an ITC on up to 50% of its capital cost, claimed in two equal 25% tranches across two statutory evaluation periods: (1) First-Term SUE (Line 504) adds 25% of the capital cost to qualified expenditures in the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after the equipment was acquired and became available for use, provided the equipment was used primarily (>50% of operating time) for SR&ED during that initial window; and (2) Second-Term SUE adds a further 25% of the capital cost to qualified expenditures in the first taxation year that ends at least 24 months after the equipment was acquired and became available for use, provided the equipment continued to be used primarily (>50% of operating time) for SR&ED across the 24-month period.
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payment Reductions

Under subsections 127(9), 127(18), 127(19), and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date of the income tax return for the taxation year.

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) (linking with paragraph 12(1)(x) inducement rules) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, including funding distributed by a non-profit organization that itself receives funding from a government body. Consequently, federal innovation grants (such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program [NRC IRAP] contributions or Strategic Innovation Fund grants) and all provincial/territorial R&D tax credits and grants (including the Ontario OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC, the Quebec CRIC, the BC SR&ED credit, and the Alberta IEG) reduce the federal qualified expenditure base dollar-for-dollar in the year earned, whereas the federal SR&ED ITC itself is excluded from the definition of government assistance for the current year and reduces the Section 37 pool in the following year. Non-government assistance encompasses analogous grants, subsidies, reimbursements, or inducements received from private or commercial entities.

A "contract payment" is defined in subsection 127(9) as an amount paid or payable to a claimant by a "taxable supplier" (generally a corporation, individual, or partnership resident in Canada or carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada, excluding tax-exempt entities) for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to deduct the amount as a current SR&ED expenditure or third-party payment. This mechanism prevents two Canadian taxpayers from claiming SR&ED tax credits on the exact same R&D work: the Canadian payer claims 80% of the contract expenditure, while the Canadian contractor must deduct the contract payment received from its own SR&ED expenditure pool. Conversely, if a Canadian R&D performer is paid by a foreign corporation that does not carry on business through a permanent establishment in Canada (meaning the foreign payer is not a "taxable supplier"), the payment is not a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), allowing the Canadian contractor to claim SR&ED ITCs on the R&D work it performs in Canada for its foreign customer. Where assistance or contract payments in respect of a project exceed the SR&ED expenditures on that project or involve related parties, subsections 127(19) and 127(20) mandate the allocation of the excess reduction across non-arm's-length parties via Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), while any subsequent repayment of government or non-government assistance restores the expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and generates an ITC addition under subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8).
Governing Bodies, Administrative Filing Procedures, and Updated Form T661 Architecture
Canada Revenue Agency Administration, CORTAX Screening, and Pre-Claim Advisory Services

Unlike dual-agency jurisdictions where a science ministry adjudicates technical eligibility and a revenue authority processes tax returns, the federal SR&ED programme is administered end-to-end by a single federal agency: the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Within the CRA's regional Tax Services Offices (TSOs), SR&ED claims are evaluated by two specialized cadres working in tandem: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), who are scientists, engineers, and computer technology specialists responsible for evaluating whether claimed projects satisfy the technical definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1); and Financial Reviewers (FRs), who are tax auditors responsible for verifying expenditure eligibility, T4 payroll records, specified employee caps, contractor nexus, and corporate schedules under Sections 37 and 127.

When a taxpayer files an SR&ED claim, all prescribed schedules—Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, Form T2038-IND, Form T1174, Form T1145, Form T1146, and Form T1263—form an integral part of the T1, T2, or T3 income tax return. Approximately 80% of all SR&ED claims are transmitted electronically, where the form data is loaded automatically onto the CRA's CORTAX mainframe system at the regional Tax Centres, while the remaining 20% of paper-filed claims are keyed manually into CORTAX. At the Tax Centre, assessors verify only whether the prescribed form fields are complete rather than auditing technical correctness, and T2 corporate claims undergo an automated preliminary risk assessment driven by the CRA's internal SR&ED Risk Management Tool, which automatically generates case files in the Audit Information Management System (AIMS). Approximately 40% of corporate T2 SR&ED claims are accepted as filed directly through this automated preliminary risk assessment without human technical review, whereas the remaining 60% of corporate claims—alongside T1 individual claims above dollar thresholds, partnership claims, and T3 trust claims—are routed to regional Tax Services Offices for manual screening and in-depth technical and financial review. For refundable claims accepted as filed without audit, the CRA's published service standard is 60 calendar days (achieved on 95% of such claims in 2025–2026), whereas claims selected for review carry a service standard of 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim, with contested technical reviews frequently spanning 12 to 18 months from fiscal year-end to final resolution. Alongside the enactment of Bill C-15, the CRA announced administrative processing reforms aimed at cutting typical SR&ED claim processing times by approximately 50%.

To enhance upfront certainty and reduce compliance friction, the CRA operates an integrated suite of pre-claim advisory services and digital portals. Claimants can access the online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) to test project eligibility anonymously without transmitting or saving any data with the CRA. Launched on June 29, 2016, the Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) provides a free, on-demand service allowing businesses to obtain an informal opinion from a CRA Research and Technology Advisor on whether ongoing R&D work qualifies as SR&ED prior to filing. Going a step further, the Pre-Claim Review (PCR)—launched on August 2, 2016 and also referred to as pre-claim approval—provides a comprehensive, free, on-demand review prior to filing that determines the exact extent of eligible R&D work and qualifying expenditures, giving businesses upfront assurance that their claim will be accepted as filed; to apply for pre-claim approval, a business must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, have gross business income under $25 million, and be in good standing with the CRA. For new or ongoing participants, the CRA also operates the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) and the optional SR&ED Service Visit (made permanent on June 20, 2023), where CRA representatives meet with claimants to review record-keeping and programme requirements. For digital file transmission during reviews, while the primary CRA portals (My Business Account, My Account, and Represent a Client) remain mandatory first-choice channels, the SR&ED programme onboarded to the browser-based Secure Drop Zone on January 15, 2024 to enable near real-time encrypted document exchange.
Statutory Filing Deadlines, Exempt Corporations, and Claim Preparer Penalties

The statutory deadline for filing an SR&ED claim is an absolute legal bar governed by subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act and detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy. While subsection 150(1) requires a corporation to file its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return within 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation has an additional 12 months after its T2 filing due date—totalling exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred—to file prescribed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 fiscal year-end faced a firm SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2026; a corporation with a December 31, 2025 year-end must file by June 30, 2027; and a corporation with a June 30, 2026 year-end must file by December 31, 2027. A corporation may file its standard T2 return by the 6-month deadline and subsequently submit Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 via an amended T2 return at any time up to the 18-month reporting deadline. Similarly, if a claimant discovers errors or additional eligible projects after submitting an initial claim, it may file an amended Form T661 to add projects or expenditures only before the 18-month deadline expires. Once the 18-month statutory window closes, any unfiled SR&ED claim or omitted expenditure is permanently statute-barred, and neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses legal authority to grant an extension.

Unincorporated individuals, trusts, and tax-exempt corporations are subject to distinct statutory filing timelines based on their respective income return due dates. Because an individual carrying on a sole proprietorship has a T1 filing due date of June 15 of the following calendar year, adding the 12-month SR&ED reporting window yields a firm deadline of June 15 of the second calendar year (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end) to file Form T661 and Form T2038-IND. Because a trust must file its T3 return within 90 days after its taxation year-end, its SR&ED filing deadline is 15 months (90 days plus 12 months) after the trust's year-end. Furthermore, under subsection 149(7) of the Income Tax Act, a corporation exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) (such as a non-profit R&D organization) that incurs SR&ED expenditures must file Form T661 on or before the due date for filing its return of income for the year—6 months after the end of its taxation year—or be subject to a statutory late-filing penalty.

Since January 1, 2014, every SR&ED claimant has also been legally required under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act to complete Part 9 of Form T661 disclosing complete information about any third-party claim preparer who accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim. Part 9 requires the claim preparer's name, Business Number or Social Insurance Number, billing arrangement code (such as contingency fee, flat fee, or hourly billing—with Canadian market contingency fees typically ranging between 15% and 25% of the approved credit), billing rates, and total fee charged. Under the CRA's Total Qualified Expenditures Policy, professional fees paid to prepare an SR&ED claim are a prescribed expenditure that cannot be included in qualified SR&ED expenditures. If required claim preparer information on Form T661 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable for a strict $1,000 statutory penalty.
Line-by-Line Technical and Financial Architecture of Updated Form T661 (26) and Schedule T2SCH31

In May 2026 (with Form T661 and Form T1145 released on May 15, 2026, Schedule T2SCH31 and the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy and Total Qualified Expenditure Policy released on May 22, 2026, Schedule T2SCH49 released on May 29, 2026, and supplemental instructions published on October 7, 2026), the CRA rolled out updated Form T661 (26) to incorporate the legislative reforms enacted through Bill C-15 while Guide T4088 undergoes formal revision. Every claimant must submit a completed Form T661 containing project-by-project technical narratives in Part 2 (up to the administrative ceiling of the 20 largest projects where a claimant undertakes more than 20 projects in a year) and financial pool schedules in Parts 3 through 6, while corporations must simultaneously file Schedule T2SCH31 to compute the resulting Investment Tax Credit or ITC recapture.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes and Federal Stacking Mechanics

Virtually every Canadian province and the Yukon Territory supplements the federal SR&ED framework with a regional R&D tax credit or statutory grant, leaving only the Northwest Territories and Nunavut without standalone territorial R&D tax credits (while Prince Edward Island utilizes discretionary innovation grants rather than a statutory tax credit schedule). Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal Income Tax Act, they reduce both the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base dollar-for-dollar in the taxation year earned. However, when a taxpayer elects the federal Prescribed Proxy Method (55% PPA), provincial R&D credits apply only to direct eligible expenditures (or direct salaries in Quebec) without adding a provincial proxy overhead amount, whereas the federal 55% PPA is calculated on the unreduced T4 salary base before provincial government assistance is subtracted at the bottom of Part 4 of Form T661. Consequently, letting Q denote total federal qualified expenditures prior to provincial assistance (including the 55% PPA on salaries), P denote the provincial tax credit earned in the year, and r denote the applicable federal ITC rate, the combined federal-provincial tax credit recovery is governed by the interaction formula:
Combined recovery = P + r × (Q − P)

Because the federal 55% PPA expands the federal cost base on direct T4 salaries to 155%, stacking a 35% federal CCPC credit with provincial refundable credits in jurisdictions such as Quebec, Ontario, or Atlantic Canada frequently yields an effective cash recovery exceeding 50% to 65% of direct R&D salary outlays.
Quebec: The CRIC Consolidation Revolution, Exclusion Thresholds, and E-Business (CDAE / CDAEIA) Credits

Unlike Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, the Atlantic provinces, and the Yukon—whose corporate R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA via the federal T2 return—Quebec administers an autonomous corporate tax regime through Revenu Québec (and Investissement Québec for technical eligibility certificates) under the Taxation Act (Quebec) via the CO-17 corporate income tax return.

To audit Quebec claims accurately, practitioners must distinguish between the historical fragmented regime (applicable to taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025) and the newly enacted CRIC regime (applicable to taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025). From 2008 through March 25, 2025, Quebec operated four separate refundable R&D tax credits: the R&D Salaries and Wages Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.7), the University Research or Public Research Centre Tax Credit (covering 80% of eligible contract amounts), the Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research Tax Credit (covering 100% of current expenses and 80% of subcontracts), and the Research Consortium Fees and Dues Tax Credit (covering 100% of contributions). Under that legacy regime, the credit rate was 30% for qualifying SMEs (phasing out linearly as global corporate assets rose between $50 million and $75 million) on up to $3 million of eligible R&D salaries/expenditures, and 14% for large businesses or excess expenditures, with arm's-length Quebec subcontractors included at 50% of the contract value. Furthermore, pursuant to Quebec Information Bulletin 2014-11 (effective for taxation years beginning after December 2, 2014), the legacy salary credit enforced an "exclusion threshold" ranging from $50,000 for SMEs up to $225,000 for large corporations, whereby the first dollars of R&D expenditure below the exclusion threshold earned zero tax credit. Additional legacy boutique credits included the Tax Credit for Industrial Design (24% for SMEs and 12% for large businesses) and the Tax Credit for Technology Adaptation Services (40% on 80% of fees paid to a College Centre for Technology Transfer [CCTT] or liaison service).

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, pursuant to the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget Plan, Quebec abolished and consolidated those four legacy R&D tax credit programmes into a single, unified, 100% refundable incentive: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC). The CRIC reform introduced three transformative changes to Quebec's innovation landscape. First, CRIC eliminated asset-based SME size restrictions entirely, establishing a universal two-tier refundable rate structure available equally to early-stage startups and multinational enterprises: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier (representing a 6-percentage-point increase over the legacy 14% base rate). For example, a company with $2 million in net eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold earns $500,000 in refundable CRIC support ($300,000 at 30% on the first $1 million plus $200,000 at 20% on the second $1 million) in addition to federal SR&ED credits. Second, CRIC expanded the scope of eligible activities beyond traditional SR&ED to include pre-commercialization activities (such as product design, regulatory testing, prototype validation, and commercialization bridging) as well as capital expenditures for R&D laboratory equipment, software development infrastructure, and prototyping machinery acquired for use in Quebec. Third, CRIC modernized the exclusion threshold calculation: instead of the asset-based $50,000 to $225,000 sliding scale, the CRIC exclusion threshold is now the greater of $50,000 or the Quebec Basic Personal Amount per employee ($18,571 in the 2025 benchmark calculation), prorated strictly by the percentage of each employee's working time spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities (for instance, 10 full-time R&D employees at $18,571 generates a $185,710 exclusion threshold). Notably, Quebec legislative provisions specify that the Quebec IP Box nexus ratio is not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold.

In addition to SR&ED and CRIC, Quebec operates the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE)—and its modernized artificial intelligence stream (CDAEIA)—administered jointly by Investissement Québec and Revenu Québec. Whereas SR&ED and CRIC target experimental development and pre-commercialization, CDAE rewards commercial software design, testing, digital platform maintenance, and AI integration in Quebec's information technology sector. To qualify for CDAE, a corporation must derive at least 75% of its gross revenue from IT activities (with at least 50% tied to software or digital product development), maintain at least 6 eligible full-time technical employees in Quebec, and apply to Investissement Québec for mandatory annual company and employee eligibility certificates within 15 months following the end of its fiscal year (whereas the SR&ED filing deadline with Revenu Québec is 18 months); failing to obtain the Investissement Québec certificate before filing the Quebec tax return automatically disqualifies the CDAE claim. Under 2024 rules, CDAE provided a 30% total tax credit (24% refundable and 6% non-refundable) on eligible technical salaries capped at $83,333 per employee (yielding a maximum credit of $25,000 per employee). Under the 2025+ CDAE / CDAEIA reforms, Quebec eliminated the $83,333 salary cap per employee, introduced a per-employee exclusion threshold aligned with the basic personal amount, and adjusted the 30% total credit split toward 20% refundable and 10% non-refundable. Quebec software and AI enterprises routinely claim both SR&ED/CRIC and CDAE/CDAEIA in the same fiscal year on distinct activity segments, and can further utilize Quebec's 5-year Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Foreign Experts, which exempts 100% of a qualifying foreign specialist's personal income in Years 1 and 2, 75% in Year 3, 50% in Year 4, and 25% in Year 5.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Triple-Stacking Framework

Corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario that perform SR&ED in Ontario can stack up to three distinct provincial tax credits administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario).

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) is an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, generating up to $240,000 in annual cash refunds. (Auditors must note that while certain third-party commercial blogs erroneously conflate OITC with OBRITC's 20% rate, authoritative CRA provincial guidance confirms the statutory OITC rate is 8%). The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is shared across an associated corporate group and phases out linearly when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income rises between $500,000 and $800,000 or when its prior-year taxable paid-up capital rises between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016, with a 2018 budget proposal for a 5.5% incremental rate over $1 million never enacted into current CRA rates) available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment regardless of size or CCPC status, with no expenditure cap, applied against Ontario corporate income tax payable (and eligible for 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward).

The Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedule 568) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an approved Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute—up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 shared across an associated group (excluding any expenditure that funds salary or wages of an ERI employee connected to the claimant corporation). Because Ontario R&D credits do not reduce each other directly as assistance (save that OITC and OBRITC reduce the ORDTC expenditure base), but all three Ontario credits constitute government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED deductible and qualified expenditure pools in the year earned, Ontario law permits a corporation to formally waive all or part of the OITC or ORDTC by filing a written waiver with its T2 return within 6 months of year-end (or on an amended return). Pre-revenue Ontario CCPCs with no Ontario tax payable frequently waive the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC so that it does not erode their 35% refundable federal cash credit.
Western Canada: British Columbia SR&ED Credit, Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

Across Western Canada, four distinct provincial regimes interact with the federal SR&ED baseline. In British Columbia, the CRA administers the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666) under Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), which provides a 10% tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in BC by a corporation with a BC permanent establishment. For qualifying CCPCs, the 10% BC credit is 100% refundable up to the corporation's expenditure limit ($3 million provincial cap, subject to taxable income and capital phase-outs), whereas for non-CCPCs and for CCPC expenditures above the limit, the 10% credit is non-refundable and can be carried back 3 years or carried forward 10 years against BC corporate tax.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29) is administered independently by the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1. Applicable to eligible expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 matching federal SR&ED qualified expenditures, the IEG must be claimed on the Alberta AT1 return within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (21 months after fiscal year-end). On up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D spending, the IEG provides a two-tier 100% refundable payment: (1) an 8% base payment on eligible R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (defined as the corporation's average eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the preceding two taxation years; if prior two-year history is unavailable, only the 8% base rate applies); and (2) an enhanced 20% incremental payment on eligible R&D spending that exceeds the prior two-year average base level. The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out linearly as the corporation's (and associated group's) prior-year federal taxable capital rises from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000, and any IEG earned reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure pool as government assistance (with a corresponding Alberta tax recapture mechanism if underlying property is disposed of).

In Manitoba, the CRA administers the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit (Schedule 380), which equals 15% of eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Manitoba after April 11, 2017 (reduced from 20% prior to that date). For in-house SR&ED carried out in Manitoba, one-half of the credit (an effective 7.5% rate) is refundable, while the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years); however, if the R&D is performed under a contract with an eligible Manitoba post-secondary educational or research institute, 100% of the 15% credit is refundable. In Saskatchewan, the CRA administers the Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit (Schedule 403 / 402) at a rate of 10% on eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures; since 2017, the 10% credit is 100% refundable for CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures (up to $100,000 cash refund), while CCPC expenditures above $1,000,000 and all expenditures by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit up to a combined $10,000,000 annual expenditure cap.
Atlantic Provinces and Yukon: Fully Refundable Regional Incentives

The Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301), along with the Yukon Territory (Schedule 442), offer the most straightforward regional stacking profiles in Canada. Administered by the CRA via the T2 corporate return (and T1 where applicable in the Yukon and Newfoundland), each of these four jurisdictions provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred within the respective province or territory, with no upper expenditure cap and full cash refundability extended to all eligible corporations regardless of size or foreign ownership. Furthermore, the Yukon Territory provides an additional 5% refundable bonus credit—for a combined 20% fully refundable rate—on eligible R&D payments made to Yukon University (formerly Yukon College).
